paragraphs: Bayesian optimisation searches for good inputs to a function that is expensive to evaluate. In high dimensions, splitting the function into smaller components can make this search more manageable. The difficulty is choosing a decomposition that represents the function across the search space. This paper shows that learning decompositions from observed data can favor patterns that work locally but fail more broadly.

The authors instead study decomposition sampling rules that do not depend on the observations. They establish theoretical guarantees for a random tree-based sampler that balances two considerations: how much information the search can gain and how much the decomposed model differs from the true function. This analysis motivates the random decomposition upper-confidence bound algorithm, RDUCB.

RDUCB achieves substantial empirical improvements over previous leading methods across the reported benchmarks. Integrating its modelling component into HEBO also improves results on the highest-dimensional Bayesmark tasks. These findings support random decomposition as a useful, easily integrated alternative, without establishing that it is sufficient for every high-dimensional optimisation problem.
icml-2023-are-random-decompositions-all-.tldr: Random tree-based decompositions provide theoretical guarantees and strong empirical results for high-dimensional Bayesian optimisation.

paragraphs: Training a classifier requires a loss that translates label information into a learning signal. When labels are uncertain, treating every example identically can overlook differences in reliability. This paper studies label-distributionally robust losses, which represent uncertainty by considering worst-case distributional weights over labels. The resulting framework connects cross-entropy, SVM losses, and related variants.

The analysis also covers temperature-scaled cross-entropy and establishes top-k consistency for LDR losses. This concerns whether optimizing the loss supports choosing the correct set of k class predictions. A complementary impossibility result identifies a tension: a loss that is both top-1 consistent and symmetric robust cannot also be top-k consistent for every k of at least two.

The authors develop an adaptive loss that adjusts a separate temperature parameter to each example’s label noise. Across seven benchmark datasets with noisy and clean settings, comparisons with thirteen losses show stable, competitive performance; evaluation also includes a real-world noisy dataset. The contribution combines a unified theoretical account with a practical way to adapt learning to uneven label uncertainty.
icml-2023-label-distributionally-robust-.tldr: Label-distributionally robust losses unify familiar classification objectives and adapt each example’s temperature to its label uncertainty.

paragraphs: Clustering becomes harder when groups have different shapes. Mixture models can represent this heterogeneity, but fitting them involves difficult objectives with undesirable local maxima. The familiar expectation-maximization algorithm can encounter such problems even for relatively simple Gaussian mixtures. This paper extends semidefinite programming approaches to clustering settings with heterogeneous groups.

The proposed iterative likelihood adjusted SDP method treats cluster labels as model parameters and directly maximizes the observed likelihood. It represents assignments through separate membership matrices for each group. This formulation avoids estimating cluster centroids, a feature that supports exact label recovery when the centroids are sufficiently separated, even when their arrangement would otherwise create difficulties.

The authors report that the method is less sensitive to initialization than expectation-maximization and more stable with high-dimensional data. Their numerical experiments show lower clustering errors than several commonly used approaches, including K-means, SDP, and expectation-maximization. The recovery claim depends on separation; the broader empirical results indicate that the formulation can also be useful for practical heterogeneous clustering.
icml-2023-likelihood-adjusted-semidefini.tldr: A likelihood-adjusted semidefinite clustering method handles heterogeneous groups while reducing sensitivity to initialization.

paragraphs: Multi-instance learning assigns one label to a collection of examples, such as the slices of a patient’s CT scan. This paper studies that setting when training directly to maximize AUC. Its central obstacle is memory: standard pooling methods require backpropagation through a bag that may contain too many instances to fit on a GPU.

The authors develop stochastic pooling methods that use only a few sampled instances from each bag for an update. They express the loss on the pooled prediction as a sequence of composed functions and combine techniques for stochastic compositional optimization with nonconvex min-max optimization. Variance reduction helps control the variability introduced by sampling.

The resulting MIDAM algorithm supports both smoothed-max pooling and attention-based pooling. The authors establish a convergence rate similar to leading deep AUC maximization algorithms, giving theoretical support to the sampled updates. Experiments on conventional multi-instance and medical datasets report superior performance. The practical contribution is a way to train from large bags without requiring every instance to participate in each gradient computation.
icml-2023-provable-multi-instance-deep-a.tldr: MIDAM trains multi-instance AUC models using a few instances per bag, with convergence guarantees and strong reported results.

paragraphs: Offline model selection asks which policy to choose when only previously logged interactions are available. This is an important part of offline reinforcement learning because developing many candidate policies does not itself identify the best one. One proposed selection signal is the mean squared Bellman error of a policy’s associated Q-function, which measures a form of inconsistency in its value predictions.

Earlier attempts to use this signal produced disappointing selection results. This paper revisits those outcomes, explaining why Bellman-error approaches performed poorly and identifying conditions under which they can work well. The distinction matters: poor results from previous methods do not by themselves establish that the underlying selection criterion is unusable.

The authors also introduce an estimator of mean squared Bellman error that is more accurate than earlier methods. It delivers strong policy-selection performance across diverse discrete control tasks, including Atari games. Together, the analysis and experiments support reconsidering Bellman errors for offline selection, with attention to the conditions for success and the quality of the error estimate.
icml-2023-revisiting-bellman-errors-for-.tldr: A more accurate Bellman-error estimator and an analysis of success conditions revive its use for offline policy selection.

paragraphs: An L1 penalty encourages sparse solutions, making it useful when a model should retain only a small set of features or parameters. This paper presents spred, a way to handle an L1 constraint on a generic differentiable objective using a simple change of parameters and ordinary stochastic gradient descent. It extends earlier connections between L1 penalties and differentiable formulations with weight decay.

The theoretical contribution is an exact differentiable formulation of the L1 problem. The authors also prove that the reparameterization is benign for a generic nonconvex function. These results support using the transformed optimization problem as a principled route to the original sparsity objective, rather than merely as a heuristic that happens to produce small parameters.

The practical demonstrations cover sparse neural networks for gene selection and neural network compression. Gene selection requires finding relevant features in a very high-dimensional space, while compression seeks a smaller network representation. The reported usefulness in both tasks connects sparsity methods from conventional statistical learning with neural network training through a familiar optimization procedure.
icml-2023-spred-solving-l1-penalty-with-.tldr: Spred reformulates L1 optimization as a differentiable problem that can be trained with standard stochastic gradient descent.

paragraphs: Federated learning keeps training data with individual collaborators while sharing model weights after local training. Sharing an update that combines many training steps may appear to hide the individual gradients needed for data reconstruction. This paper investigates that presumed protection by extending gradient inversion attacks from individual gradients to accumulated weight updates.

The proposed Surrogate Model Extension uses a surrogate model informed by two-dimensional gradient-flow characteristics and the low-rank structure of local updates. These properties provide a principled basis for adapting existing inversion attacks to updates produced over many iterations. The approach therefore addresses the specific obstacle created by combining multiple local training steps.

The authors report substantially stronger reconstruction attacks and state-of-the-art performance. In a common federated learning scenario, the method runs up to one hundred times faster than the leading baseline. That is a reported maximum speedup, not a uniform factor across settings. The findings show that keeping raw data local does not eliminate the privacy risks associated with sharing trained network weights.
icml-2023-surrogate-model-extension-sme-.tldr: SME strengthens and accelerates data-reconstruction attacks on federated learning updates accumulated over multiple local steps.

paragraphs: Mixup creates training examples by interpolating between pairs of data points and their labels. A common explanation for its success emphasizes matching linear behavior between inputs and labels. This paper finds that using different interpolation parameters for features and labels can still produce similar performance, suggesting that this explanation does not fully account for Mixup’s benefits.

The authors study an alternative explanation through a feature-noise data model. Within that model, Mixup can learn features that appear rarely by mixing them with features that occur frequently. Standard training learns the common features but misses the rare ones, leading to poor generalization in the analyzed setting. The result ties the benefit to what the model learns from the data.

The analysis further indicates that most of these feature-learning benefits arise early in training. This motivates an early-stopped version of Mixup. Experiments support the theoretical findings and the effectiveness of that approach. The paper therefore offers both a conditional account of why mixing helps and a training modification derived from the timing of those benefits.
icml-2023-the-benefits-of-mixup-for-feat.tldr: Under a feature-noise model, Mixup helps learn rare features, with most benefits arising early enough to motivate early stopping.

paragraphs: Fairness evaluation often needs sensitive attributes that are unavailable because of privacy constraints. A common workaround predicts those attributes with proxy models and then evaluates fairness using the predictions. This paper shows theoretically that directly substituting proxy predictions can create a misleading impression of either fairness or unfairness.

The authors develop a different procedure that can evaluate fairness accurately using three properly identified proxies. The qualification matters: the guarantee concerns proxies satisfying the method’s identification requirements, rather than any arbitrary set of three predictors. Their analysis also shows that these proxies can be weak, so accurate fairness measurement need not require highly accurate predictions of each person’s sensitive attributes.

As an example, the paper reports using proxies with only 68.85% accuracy on COMPAS. Experiments support the theoretical analysis and demonstrate effective bias measurement and mitigation. The result offers a way to separate the quality of the overall fairness evaluation from the accuracy of individual attribute predictions, while providing an additional layer of privacy protection through weaker proxies.
icml-2023-weak-proxies-are-sufficient-an.tldr: Three properly identified weak proxies can support accurate fairness evaluation without accurately predicting every individual’s sensitive attributes.

paragraphs: Many learning problems reconstruct an unknown object from measurements while restricting the answer to a chosen model class. This paper builds a common mathematical framework for such problems. It accommodates objects in arbitrary Hilbert spaces, random linear measurements, and nonlinear model classes, allowing different reconstruction settings to be studied within the same theory.

The central guarantees relate the amount of training data to the model class needed for near-best generalization bounds. Near-best performance is relative to what the chosen class can represent. A key concept is the variation of a model class with respect to the sampling-operator distribution, which links the candidate models to the way measurements are collected.

The framework includes matrix sketching through random sampling, compressed sensing with isotropic vectors, active regression learning, and compressed sensing with generative models. Known results in these settings follow as corollaries of the broader theory. Its contribution is therefore a shared analytical foundation: apparently different learning problems can be connected through the relationship between measurements, model structure, and required data.
icml-2024-a-unified-framework-for-learni.tldr: A unified theory connects linear measurement schemes and nonlinear model classes to data requirements for near-best generalization.

paragraphs: Learning in a game involves changing strategies in response to payoffs while other players also change theirs. This paper considers games whose payoff gradients are monotone over the strategy space, with the possibility of additive noise. The aim is to find a Nash equilibrium. The abstract contrasts this setting with noiseless cases where optimistic mirror descent achieves convergence of the latest strategy iterate.

The proposed method modifies mirror descent by perturbing payoffs according to distance from an anchor strategy, called the slingshot strategy. Adaptively Perturbed Mirror Descent repeatedly updates that anchor at a predefined interval. Updating the reference strategy adjusts the magnitude of the perturbation as learning proceeds.

The authors establish guaranteed rates for finding an equilibrium in the studied setting and report significantly faster convergence in empirical demonstrations. The contribution is an adaptive use of payoff perturbations within mirror descent, with both theoretical and experimental support. The equilibrium guarantees are tied to the paper’s monotone-game setting rather than stated for arbitrary strategic interactions.
icml-2024-adaptively-perturbed-mirror-de.tldr: Updating an anchor strategy lets perturbed mirror descent find equilibria at guaranteed rates in the studied monotone games.

paragraphs: Understanding which parts of a transformer contribute to a prediction is valuable when investigating biased outputs or hallucinations. Attribution methods aim to assign relevance to those contributing parts, but covering an entire transformer faithfully and efficiently is difficult. This paper extends Layer-wise Relevance Propagation so that it can handle attention layers.

The resulting method, AttnLRP, attributes predictions to both model inputs and internal representations. That second capability matters because an explanation can examine intermediate features as well as the information originally supplied to the model. The reported computational cost is similar to a single backward pass, making broad attribution less expensive than a procedure requiring many such computations.

Evaluations span LLaMa 2, Mixtral 8x7b, Flan-T5, and vision transformers. The authors report greater faithfulness than alternative attribution methods and show that the approach enables investigation of latent representations. This opens a route toward explanations based on internal concepts. The contribution is an efficient attribution tool for studying model behavior, rather than a demonstrated remedy for the problematic outputs motivating the work.
icml-2024-attnlrp-attention-aware-layer-.tldr: AttnLRP extends relevance propagation through attention to explain transformer inputs and internal representations at roughly backward-pass cost.

paragraphs: One-shot subset selection chooses training examples once, after which the full dataset is unavailable. This makes representativeness especially important. The paper argues that choosing only diverse examples or only difficult examples can fail to preserve the joint distribution of features and labels. It also identifies subset size as an important factor that existing selection methods often overlook.

The authors propose BOSS, which balances feature similarity and label variability. A new core-set loss bound explains why diversity and difficulty should be considered together and how the selected subset’s size influences that balance. Because the bound itself is inaccessible, the method uses a practical surrogate tailored to subset size and overall difficulty.

A Beta-scoring importance function controls the balance during selection. Experiments on synthetic and real datasets support the theoretical properties and report better performance than competitive baselines. The main implication is that a useful training subset depends on the available data budget as well as sample characteristics; a fixed preference for diversity or difficulty can miss that relationship.
icml-2024-balancing-feature-similarity-a.tldr: BOSS chooses training subsets by balancing diversity and difficulty according to subset size and overall data difficulty.

paragraphs: Multi-task learning trains one model to solve several tasks together. A common training approach computes a separate gradient for each task and combines those gradients into one parameter update. This paper argues that common aggregation methods overlook differences in sensitivity across gradient dimensions: some directions allow more change, while others are more restrictive.

The authors introduce a Bayesian aggregation procedure. They place probability distributions over task-specific parameters, which induce distributions over the corresponding gradients. These distributions provide uncertainty information for individual gradient dimensions, rather than treating each task’s gradient solely as a fixed vector. The aggregation procedure incorporates that information when forming the shared update.

Experiments across a variety of datasets demonstrate benefits and report state-of-the-art performance. The contribution is a more detailed basis for reconciling the training signals of different tasks. Instead of deciding how to combine tasks only from their gradient values, the method also accounts for uncertainty associated with the dimensions of those gradients, with empirical evidence that this improves multi-task learning.
icml-2024-bayesian-uncertainty-for-gradi.tldr: Bayesian gradient aggregation uses uncertainty in individual gradient dimensions to improve shared updates for multi-task learning.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning from images requires representations that capture useful differences between states. Behavioral-distance methods try to place functionally similar states close together using a bisimulation metric. Some approaches seek a lower-dimensional representation that preserves all these distances exactly. This paper points out that such a mapping may not exist, making the objective ill-defined.

Behavioral Eigenmaps, or BeigeMaps, use a different objective: preserve local metric structure while allowing distortion in distances between more widely separated states. This relaxation encourages representations that reveal natural clusters in the state space. The resulting representations correspond to eigenfunctions of similarity kernels constructed from behavioral distances.

The authors evaluate BeigeMaps as a drop-in modification to existing reinforcement learning algorithms based on behavioral distances. They report improved policy performance. The significance is both conceptual and practical: the representation objective avoids demanding a potentially nonexistent global distance-preserving map, while the experiments show that retaining local behavioral relationships can help agents learn from high-dimensional visual observations.
icml-2024-beigemaps-behavioral-eigenmaps.tldr: BeigeMaps preserve local behavioral relationships instead of all distances, improving reported reinforcement learning performance from images.

paragraphs: Serving large language models requires substantial computation and memory, and multi-head attention can account for more than half of those requirements. This paper identifies redundancy among attention heads: different heads often focus on highly similar sets of tokens. CHAI uses that correlation as an opportunity to reduce the work performed during inference.

The method combines highly correlated heads for self-attention at runtime. It reduces both memory use and computation without requiring fine-tuning. Its memory results concern the stored key and value cache, an important distinction from a claim about reducing the entire model’s memory footprint by the same percentage.

Across OPT-66B, LLAMA-7B, and LLAMA-33B on five evaluation datasets, the authors report key-value cache memory reductions of up to 21.4% and inference speedups of up to 1.73 times. The maximum reported accuracy deviation is 3.2%. These results show an empirical tradeoff between exploiting head redundancy and preserving predictions, with the strongest savings representing observed maxima rather than guarantees for every request.
icml-2024-chai-clustered-head-attention-.tldr: CHAI combines correlated attention heads at inference time to reduce cache memory and latency without fine-tuning.

paragraphs: A question-answering model can change its answer when a prompt changes superficially, even though its meaning stays the same. The paper connects this sensitivity to preferences for characteristics such as answer position or irrelevant image features. SteerFair addresses these biases directly in the model’s internal representations during inference.

The method starts from the observation that biases often follow simple association rules, such as linking the first answer option with correctness. It constructs demonstrations of these rules using unlabeled samples and uses them to identify directions associated with bias in representation space. It then steers activation values away from those directions.

On three benchmark tasks, SteerFair substantially reduces variation in instruction-tuned model performance across prompt modifications. It exceeds a supervised baseline using one hundred labels by average margins of 10.86 accuracy points and 12.95 score points, and matches performance with five hundred labels. These findings support unlabeled representation steering as an effective approach to the tested prompt-related biases, without establishing removal of every kind of model bias.
icml-2024-discovering-bias-in-latent-spa.tldr: SteerFair uses unlabeled examples to identify internal bias directions and reduce sensitivity to superficial prompt changes.

paragraphs: Transformer models can be expensive to serve because their parameters and computations demand substantial resources. Post-training quantization reduces the precision used to represent a pretrained model. This paper introduces FrameQuant, a scheme that reaches approximately two-bit precision, with additional overhead, while reporting only a small loss in accuracy.

The method changes the representation in which quantization occurs. It uses fusion frames, a concept from harmonic analysis, rather than directly quantizing the original weights. Interpreting quantization as added noise lets the authors connect this formulation to established results on consistent recovery and robustness to noise. Closed-form denoising filters are also available if desired.

Experiments across transformer models support the promise of substantial efficiency gains from this representation. The important distinction is that very low precision is applied within the fusion-frame formulation; the reported scheme includes overhead beyond the nominal two bits. The contribution combines a practical quantization approach with a mathematical perspective explaining why the choice of representation matters when reducing numerical precision so aggressively.
icml-2024-framequant-flexible-low-bit-qu.tldr: FrameQuant quantizes fusion-frame representations of transformers to roughly two bits plus overhead with a small reported accuracy drop.

paragraphs: The paper develops differentially private algorithms for online convex optimization, where decisions are made sequentially as loss functions arrive. Their objective is to keep regret low: the accumulated loss relative to the best fixed decision in hindsight. The central advance is obtaining stronger privacy-preserving regret guarantees without requiring smooth loss functions.

Removing the smoothness requirement extends the guarantees to losses whose slopes can change abruptly. The authors establish the first private regret bounds with an optimal leading-order term for non-smooth losses. This claim concerns the leading term, rather than every part of the bound. For smooth losses, the guarantees also improve how regret depends on the problem’s dimension.

The main technical ingredient is sampling from strongly log-concave probability densities that satisfy the Log-Sobolev Inequality. This property provides concentration guarantees, controlling how much samples fluctuate. The analysis uses that concentration to obtain a better trade-off among dimension-dependent factors. The abstract reports the best known rates across practical privacy-parameter regimes, with an exception when that parameter is exceptionally small.

The algorithm also uses rejection sampling to explicitly limit how often its decision changes. This connects the privacy result to online optimization with a switching budget, where the number of allowed changes is constrained. The authors obtain improved guarantees for that setting independently of privacy requirements.
icml-2024-improved-differentially-privat.tldr: The paper improves private online convex optimization regret guarantees without requiring smooth losses, while also improving guarantees under a switching budget.

paragraphs: Language models increasingly pause generation to interact with tools, external environments, or other agents. Inference systems designed for standalone models commonly treat that pause as the end of a request. When the external interaction finishes, they start a new request and recompute context that was already processed. The paper attributes 37–40% of total model forwarding time to this redundant work.

InferCept is an inference framework designed to support these interruptions directly. It targets GPU resource waste caused by intercepted generation and uses saved memory to serve additional requests. The system contribution is to make external interactions part of the serving workflow rather than handling every return from an interaction as a fresh generation request.

The authors report overall serving throughput improvements of 1.6–2 times and twice as many completed requests per second compared with leading inference systems. These findings show that supporting the interaction pattern of augmented language models can materially improve serving efficiency. The gains concern how requests are executed and resources are managed, rather than changes to the model’s language capabilities.
icml-2024-infercept-efficient-intercept-.tldr: InferCept reduces wasted GPU work around external tool interactions, increasing reported language-model serving throughput by 1.6–2 times.

paragraphs: Transformer-based world models can improve reinforcement learning’s sample efficiency by using extended context. This paper focuses on their representations: continuous representations can make it awkward to model distinct object categories between which interpolation has no plausible meaning. DART introduces discrete abstract representations for both learning a world model and learning behavior.

The method uses a transformer decoder to model the world autoregressively and a transformer encoder to learn behavior by attending to task-relevant information in the discrete representation. It also summarizes information from earlier time steps into memory tokens. Those tokens help address partial observability, where the current observation alone does not provide all the relevant information.

On the Atari 100k benchmark, DART outperforms previous leading methods that do not use look-ahead search. It achieves a median human-normalized score of 0.790 and exceeds human performance in nine of twenty-six games. The comparison is specifically scoped to methods without look-ahead search. The results support discrete representations and memory tokens as a useful combination for sample-efficient world modelling and behavior learning.
icml-2024-learning-to-play-atari-in-a-wo.tldr: DART uses discrete world representations and memory tokens to improve Atari sample efficiency among methods without look-ahead search.

paragraphs: For a collection of points, a median query asks for the sum of distances from every point to a proposed center. Computing this quantity repeatedly involves the full collection. This paper studies how much of that collection must be retained in a weighted summary so that such costs remain approximately correct.

The summary is a coreset: a subset of the original points with weights attached. Its requirement is stronger than accurately evaluating one chosen center. It must approximate the cost for every possible center within a multiplicative factor of one plus or minus epsilon. Epsilon therefore specifies the permitted relative error across the entire family of median queries.

The authors establish matching upper and lower bounds on coreset size of order epsilon raised to minus d divided by d plus one, up to logarithmic factors. Here d is the dimension. The upper bound shows that summaries of this size suffice; the lower bound establishes the corresponding size requirement in general. Together, they characterize the accuracy-versus-summary-size tradeoff for this geometric problem.
icml-2024-optimal-coresets-for-low-dimen.tldr: Matching bounds characterize how many weighted points are needed to approximate every geometric-median cost within a chosen relative error.

paragraphs: Probabilistic generating circuits represent distributions through probability-generating polynomials. They were introduced to unify probabilistic circuits and determinantal point processes. Their apparent additional power might seem to come from this representation. This paper identifies a different source: generating circuits permit negative weights, whereas classical probabilistic circuits require nonnegative weights.

The authors show that any generating circuit over binary variables can be converted into a probabilistic circuit with negative weights, with only polynomial growth in size. This establishes that the alternative polynomial representation is not the essential source of expressiveness in that setting. Allowing signed weights is the key distinction.

The paper also examines variables with more than two possible values. It proves that extending generating circuits to these categorical variables does not preserve tractable marginalization unless NP equals P. In contrast, probabilistic circuits with negative weights that compute set-multilinear polynomials can represent such variables while retaining tractable marginalization. In this sense, the signed probabilistic-circuit framework strictly contains the generating-circuit framework and clarifies its computational boundary.
icml-2024-probabilistic-generating-circu.tldr: Negative weights explain generating circuits’ expressive power, while signed probabilistic circuits extend further with tractable categorical marginalization.

paragraphs: EEG seizure analysis needs models that are accurate enough to be useful and efficient enough to process signals in real time. Slow inference and high memory demand can prevent deployment in clinical devices. This paper introduces REST, a graph-based residual state update mechanism designed to address those computational constraints.

REST combines graph neural networks with recurrent structures. The graph component captures the non-Euclidean relationships within EEG data, while the recurrent component captures dependencies over time. Bringing these together lets the model account for both relational structure and temporal information in seizure detection and classification.

The authors report high accuracy on both tasks, ninefold faster inference than state-of-the-art models, and substantially lower memory demand than the smallest model used for the task. Those findings make REST a promising candidate for devices such as responsive neurostimulation systems or seizure alerts. The stated result is improved model efficiency and accuracy, supporting the prospect of real-time clinical implementation rather than establishing that such deployment has already been achieved.
icml-2024-rest-efficient-and-accelerated.tldr: REST combines graph and recurrent modelling for accurate EEG seizure analysis with ninefold faster reported inference and lower memory use.

paragraphs: Adversarial text attacks seek small input changes that cause a model to behave incorrectly. Changing whole tokens can inadvertently alter a sentence’s meaning, weakening the validity of the attack example. Character-level edits can more easily preserve meaning, but they have received less attention because gradient-based methods are difficult to apply and these attacks have been considered easy to defend.

The paper introduces Charmer, an efficient query-based character attack. It aims to achieve both a high attack success rate and high similarity between the original and modified text. Considering both outcomes matters: an attack is more informative when it changes model behavior while leaving the input closely related to what the model originally received.

Charmer successfully attacks both BERT and Llama 2. On BERT with SST-2, it improves attack success by 4.84 percentage points and USE similarity by eight percentage points relative to prior work. These results challenge the view that character-level perturbations are a weak threat and demonstrate that successful attacks can remain highly similar to the original examples.
icml-2024-revisiting-character-level-adv.tldr: Charmer uses character-level queries to attack language models while preserving high similarity to the original text.
